questions.text:
Choose ONE science idea from the Resource Booklet:
• Science Idea One: Developing earthquake-resistant building materials for New Zealand homes
• Science Idea Two: Using native wetland plants to filter agricultural run-off

For Part One, focus on these two features of science (FOS):
• the influence of social and cultural factors on science
• responding to needs and opportunities

(a) How does the influence of social and cultural factors on science contribute to the development of the science idea?

(b) How does responding to needs and opportunities contribute to the development of the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Identify how each FOS contributed to the science idea with examples from the resource
questions.markingGuide:
Achieved: Identify each FOS and outline how it contributed.

Idea One: (a) After the Christchurch earthquakes, public demand for safer buildings grew.

Cultural heritage concerns meant engineers needed materials that could protect both modern and historically significant structures.

(b) The devastating effects of the earthquakes created a need for stronger building materials, giving researchers opportunities to develop new concrete composites reinforced with natural fibres.

Idea Two: (a) Farming is central to New Zealand's economy and rural communities, so solutions must work alongside farming rather than replacing it.

Māori concepts of kaitiakitanga (guardianship) influenced the approach to protecting waterways.

(b) Declining water quality in rivers created an urgent need.

Researchers recognised the opportunity to use harakeke and raupō in constructed wetlands to filter nitrates and phosphates from farm run-off.

questions.text: (c) Why are these features of science important to the development of the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Explain WHY each FOS was significant, giving reasons and examples from the local context
questions.markingGuide:
Merit: Explain why each FOS was significant.

Idea One: (social/cultural) Public concern about safety after the earthquakes meant more government funding was directed to materials research — without this social pressure, the research may not have been prioritised.

Heritage buildings required solutions that preserved their character, pushing engineers to develop flexible retrofit materials.

(needs/opportunities) The destruction created an urgent need for better materials, which would not have been investigated without the earthquake events.

This gave researchers the opportunity to test ideas in real-world damaged buildings.

Idea Two: (social/cultural) Farming communities needed to maintain their livelihoods while improving water quality.

If the social factor of rural employment was ignored, a solution like removing farms entirely could have been proposed instead.

Māori cultural values provided a philosophical framework that guided the research.

(needs/opportunities) The measurable decline in river health provided the urgent need.

Researchers saw the opportunity to combine traditional plant knowledge with modern water treatment science.

questions.text: (d) How do the two features of science work together to support the development of the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Discuss how the two FOS have interacted, with detailed relationship and examples
questions.markingGuide:
Excellence: Discuss how the FOS have interacted.

Idea One: The social impact of the earthquakes (homes destroyed, communities displaced) created both the cultural motivation and the practical need for better materials.

Cultural concerns about preserving heritage buildings created specific design constraints that pushed engineers to develop flexible materials rather than simply stronger ones — responding to a more nuanced need.

The social factors defined the problem, and responding to those needs drove the research in a particular direction.

Idea Two: The cultural importance of rivers to Māori (as sources of mahinga kai) and the economic importance of farming to rural communities together defined the problem as one requiring a solution that benefits both water quality and farming.

This specific social context created the opportunity for researchers to develop constructed wetlands using native plants — a solution that would not have emerged if either the cultural or economic factors had been absent.

questions.text:
For Part Two, focus on these two features of science:
• linking new evidence to existing models, theories, and ideas
• the influence of the development and use of technology on science

(a) How does linking new evidence to existing models, theories, and ideas add to the science idea?

(b) How does the influence of the development and use of technology add to the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Identify how each FOS contributed to the science idea
questions.markingGuide:
Achieved: Identify each FOS and outline how it contributed.

Idea One: (a) Data from earthquake sensors was linked to existing structural engineering models to predict which building materials would absorb the most seismic energy.

The new fibre-reinforced concrete data was compared to existing concrete strength standards.

(b) 3D printing technology allowed engineers to rapidly prototype test panels, and shake-table simulators reproduced earthquake forces in a laboratory.

Idea Two: (a) Water quality measurements downstream of pilot wetlands were linked to existing nutrient-cycling models, showing that the plants reduced nitrate concentrations by 60%.

This confirmed existing theories about biological filtration.

(b) Automated water sensors that continuously measure nitrate and phosphate levels provided real-time data, replacing manual monthly sampling.

questions.text: (c) Why are these two features of science significant to the development of the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Explain WHY linking new evidence and the use of technology were each significant
questions.markingGuide:
Merit: Explain why each FOS was significant.

Idea One: Linking new test data to existing building codes was significant because it allowed engineers to determine whether the new materials met safety standards without rebuilding from scratch.

Shake-table technology was significant because testing real-scale building components in an earthquake simulation is safer and faster than waiting for a real event.

Idea Two: Linking the 60% nitrate reduction data to existing nutrient models was significant because it validated the effectiveness of native plant wetlands using established scientific frameworks.

Continuous water sensors were significant because they captured daily fluctuations that monthly manual testing would have missed, providing more accurate data.

questions.text: (d) How do these two features of science work together to develop the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Discuss the interaction between linking new evidence and technology in developing the science idea
questions.markingGuide:
Excellence: Discuss how the FOS have interacted.

Idea One: The shake-table technology generated new evidence about how fibre-reinforced panels behaved under simulated earthquakes.

This evidence was then linked to existing structural engineering models to predict how the materials would perform in real buildings.

Without the technology, the evidence could not have been generated;.

without the existing models, the evidence would have been difficult to interpret.

The two features are interdependent.

Idea Two: Automated water sensors generated continuous data streams that captured how nitrate levels changed hourly after rainfall events.

This high-resolution evidence was linked to existing catchment hydrology models, revealing patterns that monthly sampling would have missed.

The technology enabled the collection of evidence that refined the existing scientific models, and those models in turn guided where sensors should be placed for the most informative data.

questions.text:
For Part Three, focus on these two features of science:
• the influence of the development and use of technology on science
• responding to needs and opportunities

How do these two features of science support each other in the development of the science idea?
questions.expectedAnswer: Discuss how technology and responding to needs/opportunities have supported each other
questions.markingGuide:
Excellence: Discuss the interaction between the two FOS.

Idea One: The devastating Christchurch and Kaikōura earthquakes created an urgent need for better building materials.

This need drove investment in shake-table technology and 3D printing of test panels, which would not have been developed as quickly without the urgency.

In turn, the technology enabled researchers to test hundreds of material combinations rapidly, creating new opportunities to discover fibre-reinforced composites that exceeded existing standards.

The need drove the technology, and the technology created opportunities for solutions that went beyond the original need.

Idea Two: Declining water quality in farming regions created the need for affordable, effective filtration.

This need drove the development of automated nutrient sensors that could monitor wetland performance continuously and cheaply.

The sensor technology then created new opportunities — researchers discovered that certain combinations of raupō and harakeke were more effective at different times of year, leading to seasonal planting recommendations.

Without the need, the sensors would not have been deployed in wetlands;.

without the sensors, the seasonal patterns would not have been discovered.

Both features supported each other in advancing the science idea.
